summary: This document describes how to proxy IP packets through HTTP. Similar to UDP proxying in HTTP, it lets an HTTP client create an IP tunnel through an HTTP server that acts as an IP proxy. Arbitrary IP packets can be sent. It updates RFC 9298.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of mailing a whole parcel inside a normal web-browsing envelope. A helper opens it and forwards it, so the parcel reaches places it couldn't go alone.

questions: how does ip proxying in http work
subtitle: How an HTTP client can open a tunnel that carries whole IP packets through an HTTP server acting as an IP proxy.

tldr.problem: HTTP CONNECT can tunnel TCP, and a companion mechanism can tunnel UDP, but neither can carry other IP protocols or fields of the IP header.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a request with the connect-ip upgrade token. The server answers, and the two sides then exchange full IP packets in HTTP Datagrams, plus capsules that assign addresses and advertise routes.
tldr.outcome: One protocol supports remote access VPNs, site-to-site VPNs, single-flow forwarding and similar uses over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. It updates RFC 9298 by changing the masque well-known URI.

today: RFC 9484 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 9298, the UDP proxying document, by changing the masque well-known URI registration.

sections.title: Why Proxy IP Over HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP already has the CONNECT method for creating a TCP tunnel, and a similar mechanism for UDP. These cannot tunnel other IP protocols or convey fields of the IP header. RFC 9484 defines a way to tunnel IP itself through an HTTP server acting as an IP proxy.

The RFC lists remote access VPN, site-to-site VPN, secure point-to-point communication and general-purpose packet tunnelling as uses. It works like UDP proxying: the proxy is identified by an absolute URL built from a URI template, and the protocol covers all existing HTTP versions by using HTTP Datagrams. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use Extended CONNECT, and HTTP/1.x uses HTTP Upgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal web tunnels can only carry certain kinds of mail. This one lets you send any kind of network packet through a web server that forwards it for you.

sections.title: Templates, Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Clients are configured with a URI template that may contain two variables, target and ipproto. The template must be a level 3 template or lower, in absolute form, with the path starting with a slash. A client that finds a template breaking the rules must reject it and not send the request. Clients that can only be given a host and port can try the default template, which ends in /.well-known/masque/ip/{target}/{ipproto}/.

The request asks for the connect-ip upgrade token. With HTTP/1.1 it is a GET with Connection: Upgrade and Upgrade: connect-ip, and success is a 101 (Switching Protocols) response. With HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 it is an Extended CONNECT with :protocol set to connect-ip, and success is any 2xx status. Anything else, such as a 3xx, means the client must treat the attempt as failed. Requests and successful responses carry no message content, and the whole thing MUST run over TLS or QUIC encryption or an equivalent.

The tunnel lives as long as the request stream. The proxy keeps address and route assignments while the stream is open, and may tear the tunnel down after inactivity, but then it MUST close the stream. If the target is a DNS name, the proxy resolves it before replying and rejects the request on errors.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on the web server's door with a special password, connect-ip. If it says yes, the door stays open as long as you need and parcels can flow through.

sections.title: Limiting the Request Scope
sections.content:
Unlike UDP proxying, an IP proxying request can let endpoints send arbitrary IP packets to any host. A client may narrow a request with the two optional template variables, and if they are missing they mean the wildcard value (an asterisk).

  • target: a hostname or IP prefix. For a prefix, the request supports a single IP version. For a hostname, the proxy resolves it and SHOULD advertise routes for all resolved addresses it can reach. IPv6 colons must be percent-encoded, so 2001:db8::42 becomes 2001%3Adb8%3A%3A42, and a prefix length follows a percent-encoded slash (%2F).
  • ipproto: a decimal Internet Protocol Number from 0 to 255, or the asterisk wildcard. ICMP traffic is always allowed whatever the value.

Scoping lets the proxy optimise, for example by giving two requests scoped to different prefixes or protocols the same public address. The proxy MAY also use the scope for access control and reject a request right away. Protocol numbers that are IPv6 extension headers may be rejected, and implementations that scope by protocol number MUST walk the chain of extension headers to find the outermost non-extension protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the helper, "I only want to talk to this one house" or "I only want to send this one kind of parcel." That makes the helper's job simpler.

sections.title: Capsules and Datagrams
sections.content:
Three capsule types let the two endpoints exchange IP configuration, and either side MAY send any number of them.

  • ADDRESS_ASSIGN (type 0x01) gives the peer a list of addresses or prefixes it may use as source addresses. Each capsule holds the full current list, so an address missing from a later capsule has been removed, and an empty capsule removes all of them.
  • ADDRESS_REQUEST (type 0x02) asks the peer for addresses. Request IDs MUST NOT be zero or reused. An all-zero address means no preference. The peer SHOULD answer each request with a matching Assigned Address, and an all-zero address with the maximum prefix length means refused. A request with zero entries MUST abort the request stream.
  • ROUTE_ADVERTISEMENT (type 0x03) lists address ranges the sender will route to. Each capsule supersedes earlier ones, so ranges left out are withdrawn. Ranges must be ordered by IP version, then IP protocol, then address, with no overlap; a capsule that breaks this MUST abort the stream.

Actual traffic travels in HTTP Datagrams that begin with a Context ID, a variable-length integer. Context ID 0 is reserved for IP payloads, and then the payload is a full IP packet from the IP Version field to the last byte of the IP payload. Non-zero even IDs are allocated by the client and odd ones by the proxy, which leaves room for future extensions. An HTTP/3 datagram with an unknown Context ID is dropped or briefly buffered.
sections.plainLanguage: Capsules are little notes passed along the tunnel: "here is your address," "may I have an address," and "I can deliver to these places." The parcels themselves go in plain numbered boxes, and box 0 means an ordinary IP packet.

sections.title: How Packets Are Handled
sections.content:
The tunnel is conceptually an IP link, but not a full interface. It does not necessarily have IPv6 link-local addresses and does not use router advertisements, stateless autoconfiguration or neighbor discovery. Over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 a client MAY send packets optimistically before the response arrives, though the proxy may drop them.

When an endpoint receives a datagram it behaves like a router: it parses the IP header, applies local policy checks such as source address validation, consults its routing table and forwards or drops the packet. A failed check is a forwarding error, not a protocol violation. Endpoints decrement the Hop Count (TTL) when they encapsulate but not when they decapsulate, which prevents infinite loops. Link-local traffic must not be forwarded beyond the interface it arrived on.

IPv6 requires a link MTU of at least 1280 bytes. Endpoints that route IPv6 MUST ensure the tunnel carries at least 1280 bytes, and unless they have another guarantee they MUST use ICMPv6 echo requests with 1232 bytes of data to check, tearing down the tunnel when there is no reply. Forwarding errors SHOULD be signalled with ICMP messages carried in HTTP Datagrams, such as Destination Unreachable or Packet Too Big.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the tunnel acts like a small post office. It checks the address, decides where the parcel should go, and sends back a note if something cannot be delivered.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four set-ups, all shown over HTTP/3.

  • Remote access VPN: the client sends no scope, requests an IPv4 address, is assigned 192.0.2.11 and receives a full-tunnel route of 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255. A split-tunnel variant advertises only part of 192.0.2.0/24.
  • Site-to-site VPN: a branch network 192.0.2.0/24 and a corporate network 203.0.113.0/24 are joined, each side assigning the other an address and a route. Because the Hop Count is decremented on encapsulation, protocols that require that field to be 255 will not work.
  • IP flow forwarding: the client asks for target.example.com with ipproto=132 (SCTP) and gets one address and one scoped route.
  • Proxied connection racing: with ipproto=17 (UDP), the proxy assigns both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address and routes for the resolved addresses, so the client can run Happy Eyeballs through the proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show different jobs for the same tunnel: a laptop joining an office network, two offices joining each other, or just sending one special kind of parcel to one place.

sections.title: Performance and Extensibility
sections.content:
Extensions SHOULD define new capsule types for configuration. It is RECOMMENDED that extensions that change addressing send their capsules before ADDRESS_ASSIGN and take effect only when it is parsed, so changes happen atomically.

Running congestion-controlled or loss-recovering protocols such as TCP or QUIC inside the tunnel stacks two controllers. To avoid duplicate retransmission when the outer connection is TCP, IP proxying SHOULD be done over HTTP/3 to use the QUIC DATAGRAM frame. Endpoints SHOULD NOT queue packets to increase batching beyond what hardware offload needs. An oversized packet that cannot fit in a QUIC DATAGRAM frame SHOULD be dropped, with an ICMP Packet Too Big sent back.

If congestion control is disabled on the outer connection, the sender MUST mark outer IP headers Not-ECT. For Differentiated Services, when the outer connection is congestion-controlled, an endpoint MUST NOT copy the DSCP from the inner header to the outer one, and endpoints MUST NOT coalesce inner packets with different DSCP markings into the same outer packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending traffic through a tunnel is like having two traffic cops. The RFC asks the tunnel to avoid piling up packets and to use the faster, more modern road, HTTP/3, when it can.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Letting arbitrary clients send to arbitrary hosts is risky, because bad actors could have their traffic attributed to the proxy. Servers SHOULD restrict IP proxying to authenticated users, for example with mutual TLS, the HTTP Authorization header or bearer tokens, and can rate limit clients or limit assigned prefixes.

Address assignment can reveal which packets come from the same client, so proxies SHOULD avoid persistent per-client address assignment when possible. Where an endpoint knows its peer may only use a given prefix, it MUST follow BCP 38 to prevent source address spoofing. A proxy that shares one external address between clients scoped to different protocols and forwards ICMP MUST inspect the invoking packet and forward the message only to the matching client. Copying DSCP values to the outer header can expose a flow and is NOT RECOMMENDED in privacy-sensitive contexts.

Optimistic sending is not allowed in HTTP/1.x, because a server that rejected the Upgrade might parse the packets as a new HTTP request, enabling request smuggling.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel that goes anywhere is a risk, so the helper should only let known people use it, and should not hand out the same labels in ways that let others track you.
